editorial:
The Phantom Express is a 50-minute silent crime-railroad picture released in November 1925 by Banner Productions and distributed in the United States by Henry Ginsberg Distributing Company (and in the UK by Wardour Films). Director John G. Adolfi led a cast including Ethel Shannon, David Butler, and a young Frankie Darro through an original scenario written by Tom J. Hopkins â€” a devoted railroad engineer seizes the throttle of his company's fastest locomotive after his sweetheart's father is broken by a wreck, with criminal interference (George Siegmann as villain Rufus Hardy) threatening the run. The 95-year US copyright term on the 1925 print expired January 1, 2021, placing the footage definitively in the public domain whether or not Banner Productions ever filed a renewal in 1952â€“53.

The live rights trap for anyone using a circulating copy is the musical score layer. Silent prints are nearly always distributed with some accompaniment, and any score newly composed or performed for a modern release carries its own separate copyright, wholly independent of the PD image track. If the score was composed after 1928 or recorded after 1972, that audio layer is still protected. Reusers should either verify that a copy's accompaniment derives from pre-1929 sheet music performed before the sound-recording cutoff, commission a new live performance of period-appropriate public-domain music, or mute and replace the audio before distributing their version.

That depends on when the score was composed and recorded, and it is separate from the film copyright. Any musical accompaniment added to a modern circulating print is its own protected work if it was composed after 1928 and recorded after 1972.
